data.cultural_impact: The name Lucianina carries a rich cultural heritage from both the Roman and Christian traditions. In its Roman roots, it evokes images of patriarchal leadership, strength, and noble Roman heritage. Meanwhile, its Christian origins highlight the spiritual value in devotion, faith, and selflessness - traits symbolized by Saint Lucian. Today, it serves as a powerful reminder of the interconnectedness of culture and spirituality.
data.spiritual_significance: Lucianina holds deep spiritual significance, named after Saint Lucian, it represents a connection to the divine despite hardships. Saint Lucian, having the nickname "the Confessor," was a bishop who underwent persecution during the Roman Empire. Showing unwavering strength and courage, he shone as a beacon of faith and devotion. Carrying this moniker honors the value of maintaining moral and spiritual grounding in the midst of adversity, resonating with the meaning of the name itself: light or shining one.

historical_references.reference: According to legend, Lucianina was a Christian virgin martyr who lived in Syracuse, Sicily during the time of Emperor Diocletian (late 3rd century AD). She was tortured and killed for her faith, but miraculously survived the ordeal and was later healed by Saint Agatha. Lucianina is venerated as a patron saint of Sicily, particularly in the towns of Palermo and Monreale.

Another version of the story of Lucianina comes from the town of Monreale, Sicily. According to this account, Lucianina was a wealthy and beautiful noblewoman who converted to Christianity during the reign of Emperor Maxentius (early 4th century AD). She was betrayed by her husband and handed over to the authorities for her faith. Lucianina was tortured and put on trial, but refused to deny her beliefs. She was sentenced to be burnt at the stake, but miraculously survived the flames. After this, she was beheaded and her body was buried in a cave. Her tomb became a site of pilgrimage, and a church was built over it in the 12th century.
